property_summary: For every admissible input where transfer(...) completes (does not revert), the reference contract C always returns true; the mutant returns false for some inputs, so the returned boolean differs.

For any non-empty _tos array and matching v array length, C.transfer(...) always returns true when the call completes; the mutant sometimes returns false for the same inputs, so the returned boolean differs.

For every non-empty _tos array with matching v length where all external calls to caddress succeed, C.transfer(...) returns true (completes and returns true); the mutant returns false for the same admissible inputs, breaking that rule.

For any non-empty _tos array and matching v array length where the callee at caddress always succeeds on the transferFrom selector, C.transfer(...) always completes and returns true; the mutant returns false for the same admissible inputs.

For any non-empty _tos array with matching v length where the callee at caddress always succeeds for the transferFrom selector, C.transfer(...) always returns true (the mutant returns false for the same inputs), so the reference's returned boolean is true while the mutant can return false.

Rule: C.transfer never changes C's own storage or observable state when invoking external contracts; the mutant using delegatecall can execute callee code in C's context and thus can modify C's state (breaking the rule for some inputs).

Calling transfer(...) never allows the callee to modify C's public state (reference preserves C's state across external calls), but replacing call with delegatecall lets a malicious callee mutate C's storage for some inputs, so the mutant can change a public getter value while the reference cannot.

For any inputs, calling transfer(...) never changes C's own public uint state variable `transfer` (reference preserves C's storage across external calls); the mutant using delegatecall allows a callee to modify C.transfer for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any inputs, calling C.transfer(...) never causes C's own public uint slot 0 to change (reference preserves C's storage across external calls); the mutant using delegatecall can let a malicious callee mutate C's storage (observable via a public getter) for some inputs, violating the rule.

For any inputs, calling C.transfer(...) never causes the callee's code to be executed in C's context so it cannot change C's observable behavior; replacing call with delegatecall lets a malicious callee execute in C's context and thus can make C.transfer revert (or change observable behavior) for some inputs.

For any inputs, C.transfer(...) succeeds (does not revert) when the target callee implements transferFrom as a non-state-mutating view that returns normally; replacing call with staticcall can cause the external transferFrom to revert when it attempts state mutation, so the mutant may make transfer(...) revert for some callee/inputs.

For any callee address that implements transferFrom as a non-mutating view (i.e., does not attempt state changes), C.transfer(...) always succeeds (returns/does not revert); replacing call with staticcall can cause calls that perform state mutations to revert, so there exist callee implementations and inputs for which the mutant makes transfer(...) revert while the reference still succeeds.

For any inputs with a non-empty _tos array, C.transfer always returns (does not revert) when each callee's transferFrom may perform state writes; replacing call with staticcall can make such external calls revert, so the mutant can cause transfer to revert for some callee and inputs.

For any non-empty _tos array and any target contract that implements transferFrom by performing an internal state write then returning normally, C.transfer never reverts (always returns true); changing call to staticcall can cause the external transferFrom (which writes state) to revert under staticcall, so the mutant may make transfer revert for some fuzzed inputs.

For any non-empty _tos array and any callee address, the reference C.transfer always returns true (does not revert) when calling a target that itself performs a state-changing transferFrom; replacing call with staticcall can make that external transferFrom revert under staticcall, causing transfer to revert — so the property: C.transfer never reverts for any inputs where the callee's transferFrom performs a state write and returns normally, but the mutant may revert.

For all calls, C.transfer must revert when passed an empty _tos array (i.e., it must not silently accept empty arrays); the mutant removed that require and therefore accepts empty _tos, breaking the rule.

For every input, the reference C reverts (call fails) when transfer is invoked with an empty _tos array, while the mutant accepts empty _tos and returns true; the test fuzzes the arrays and asserts that calling transfer with the given parameters reverts exactly when _tos is empty (so the reference always reverts for empty arrays but the mutant does not).

For all inputs, C.transfer(...) reverts when given two arrays of different lengths (mismatched _tos and v), because it indexes v[i] assuming equal length; the mutant still compiles but by removing the require about non-empty arrays it allows empty arrays but still would behave same for length mismatch—however the concrete difference is that when lengths differ, reference will revert due to out-of-bounds access when v shorter than _tos; we assert that transfer reverts whenever _tos.length != v.length (reference always reverts for that domain), and the mutant (which removed only the non-empty check) will be exposed if it fails to revert for some mismatched-length input.

For every call to transfer, the reference C requires that when both _tos and v are empty the call reverts (it does not accept empty recipient arrays); the mutant removed that require and will accept empty arrays and return true, so the property is that transfer(...) reverts iff _tos.length == 0 (reference: always reverts for empty _tos), which the mutant violates for some fuzzed inputs (empty arrays).

For any non-empty _tos array, reference C always reverts the entire transfer call if any external transferFrom call fails; the mutant ignores failed external calls allowing transfer(...) to return true even when some external calls failed.
